stem: In the figure shown, line r is parallel to line s. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both marked angles are drawn in the same corner of their crossing - between the upward-right part of t and the rightward part of the horizontal line - so they are corresponding angles. A transversal across parallel lines makes corresponding angles equal, so x = 44. None of the printed choices is 44, so this question as printed has no correct option.

whyWrong.A: 30 is not equal to 44 and no relationship in the figure produces it.
whyWrong.B: 45 is close to 44 but not equal to it; the figure gives exactly 44, and rounding an angle to a "nice" value is not a legitimate step.
whyWrong.C: 60 does not arise from 44 by any of the parallel-line relationships (equal, or 180 minus).
whyWrong.D: 90 would require the transversal to be perpendicular to both lines, which the marked 44-degree angle rules out.

note: DEFECT: the correct value is 44 and it is not among the printed choices A) 30, B) 45, C) 60, D) 90. The two marked angles occupy identical corresponding positions, so x must equal 44. Needs a human decision - most likely the choice block belongs to a different question. Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, r above and s below, crossed by a line t rising from lower left to upper right; x is marked above r to the right of t and 44 degrees is marked above s to the right of t, both with the same arc.

stem:
\[ g(x) = \frac{1}{11}\left(5(2)^{x} + 4\right) \]

The function g is defined by the given equation. For all values of x, the value of g(x) is greater than k, where k is a constant. What is the greatest possible value of k?
whyCorrect: \( 2^{x} \) is always positive but gets arbitrarily close to 0 as x becomes very negative, so \( 5(2)^{x} + 4 \) is always above 4 and approaches 4. Dividing by 11, g(x) is always above \( \frac{4}{11} \) and gets as close to it as you like, so the greatest possible k is \( \frac{4}{11} \) . That value is not correctly printed among the choices.

whyWrong.A: 4 forgets to divide by 11; g(x) is under 1 for very negative x, so it is not always above 4.
whyWrong.B: As printed, \( \frac{4}{1} \) is just 4, so it repeats choice A. It appears to be a misprint of \( \frac{4}{11} \) .
whyWrong.C: 9 is larger still and is not a value the function stays above.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{9}{11} \) uses 5 + 4 = 9 in the numerator, as if \( 2^{x} \) were fixed at 1; the horizontal asymptote comes from \( 2^{x} \to 0 \) , not \( 2^{x} = 1 \) .

note: DEFECTIVE. The correct answer, 4/11, is printed as choice B in the form 4/1, which equals 4 and therefore duplicates choice A. Almost certainly a dropped digit in the book's typesetting; fix choice B to 4/11 before importing.

stem: \[(x+3)^{2}+(y-18)^{2}=169\]The graph of the given equation is a circle in the xy-plane. The point (a, b) lies on the circle. Which of the following is a possible value for a?
whyCorrect: The circle has center (-3, 18) and radius \(\sqrt{169}=13\), so the x-coordinate of any point on it satisfies \(-3-13 \le a \le -3+13\), that is \(-16 \le a \le 10\). Every one of -16, -10, 3 and 10 falls in that interval, so all four are possible values of a; only 16 lies outside the circle's horizontal reach. As printed, the question has four correct answers.
note: DEFECTIVE as printed. Five choices are given (A-E, itself non-standard) and four of them - -16, -10, 3 and 10 - are all possible x-coordinates, since a can be anything in [-16, 10]. Only E (16) is impossible. Either the choices need replacing (the real SAT version would offer one value inside [-16, 10] and three outside) or the stem should read 'which is NOT a possible value', in which case the answer is E. No answer recorded because there is no unique one.
